humanities_role_explanation: The study targets iconographic classification: identifying Christian saints in paintings by their attributes, using Iconclass codes. This is an art-historical competence, not generic image classification on art data. The paper frames iconography as a 'branch of the history of art' and positions the models as metadata-curation tools for digital humanities workflows.
benchmark_modalities_explanation: Images of paintings are the primary input. They are paired with text prompts listing candidate class labels (Test 1) or Iconclass descriptions (Test 2). Test 3 adds five labelled exemplar images. The CSV metadata's 'text' only modality understates this.
analytical_tasks_explanation: The task is single-label 'iconographic classification' of Christian saints. Paintings are assigned to one of the 10 most frequent Iconclass saint classes per dataset. Three conditions are tested: zero-shot with label names, zero-shot with Iconclass descriptions ('possible attributes: book (or scroll), crown ...'), and few-shot with five exemplars. Recognising saints by their attributes is the iconographic level of identification. It is scored as closed-set classification, not as open hermeneutic interpretation, so 'interpretation' is not included.

general_purpose_benchmark.note: Scoped to a single task, single-label classification of Christian saints, in one domain.

evaluates_generative_llm.note: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 2.5 Pro and Gemini 2.5 Flash. Also CLIP and SigLIP variants and fine-tuned ResNet50 baselines.

quantitative_metrics.note: Accuracy, plus cross-dataset prediction consistency on 36 matched image pairs.

summary: The paper benchmarks CLIP and SigLIP vision-language models and the multimodal LLMs GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 on single-label classification of Christian saints. It uses three Iconclass-annotated datasets: ArtDL, an ICONCLASS AI Test Set subset and Wikidata. Models are tested zero-shot with labels, zero-shot with Iconclass descriptions, and few-shot, and compared against fine-tuned ResNet50 baselines.
key_findings: Gemini-2.5 Pro peaked at 90.45% on ArtDL and 84.82% on ICONCLASS, beating the ResNet50 baselines (84.44% and 40.46%). On Wikidata, SigLIP-so400m was best at 66.29%, while the LLMs stayed around 44-47%. Iconclass descriptions generally helped zero-shot performance, and few-shot mostly lowered accuracy. LLMs showed low cross-dataset consistency (25-33%) compared with contrastive models. The authors suspect training-data contamination for ArtDL and ICONCLASS.
facets_explanation: No new annotation is described. The labels are the Iconclass codes already attached to images in ArtDL, the ICONCLASS AI Test Set and Wikidata (retrieved via SPARQL). The authors filtered these to the top 10 saint classes and removed multi-saint or multi-label images. In Test 1 the model receives only label names, so naming the saint requires external iconographic knowledge linking visual attributes to figures. Test 2 partly supplies that knowledge in the prompt. Scoring is top-1 match to a single label. Annotator or reading disagreement is not discussed.
results_explanation: Table 2 (ArtDL) gives 'gemini-2.5-pro-preview-05-06 90.45% 90.18% 86.59%', and the text reports 'a peak of 90.45% achieved by Gemini-2.5 Pro'. That is the headline accuracy. Tests 1-3 vary the prompt context (labels, descriptions, exemplars) and the learning setting on the same closed-set classification. They are not answer-format or difficulty-split changes, so no format gap is recorded and the gap points are null. The only baselines are fine-tuned ResNet50 models, not humans, so the human fields are null. The benchmark is mono-traditional (Christian iconography), so cultural asymmetry does not arise.

humanities_role.quote: Iconography, being that "branch of the history of art which concerns itself with the subject matter or meaning of works of art, as opposed to their form"

dataset_size.quote: The test set, published along with the paper, contains 1,864 images.

primary_evaluation_setting.quote: Models were tested under three conditions: (1) classification using class labels, (2) classification with Iconclass descriptions, and (3) few-shot learning with five exemplars.

gold_source.quote: Each image is annotated with Iconclass codes, covering 10 key figures of Christian iconography

gold_beyond_stimulus.quote: The models classify images using only class label names
This configuration tests the model’s ability to leverage pre-trained knowledge connections between visual features and semantic concepts.

answer_multiplicity.quote: Each is mapped to a single iconographic label

reported_best_score.quote: to a peak of 90.45% achieved by Gemini-2.5 Pro

review_notes: benchmark_name: ciop gave null; cip used the paper title plus dataset names. The paper presents an evaluation framework but never names a benchmark, so null. analytical_tasks: cip added 'interpretation'. Dropped, because saint identification is scored as closed-set top-1 classification (p. 5, Sec. 2.3.1), not hermeneutic reading; the paper's own term 'iconographic classification' is recorded in the explanation. relevant_asjc_areas: cip added 'History'. Dropped, because nothing in the tasks targets historical knowledge. Religious Studies is kept because the class set is Christian saints and the Iconclass descriptions carry hagiographic attributes. reported_format_gap: ciop said 'no'; cip said 'yes', 19 points, from SigLIP-base on ArtDL, Test 1 vs Test 2 (p. 7, Table 2). Resolved to 'no': Tests 1-3 enrich the prompt context or switch zero-shot to few-shot on the same closed-set classification. That is not a multiple-choice vs open-ended change, an exact vs partial match, a hard split, or an image vs text-only comparison. Confidence is low because Test 1 vs Test 2 could be read as a regime change. Other facets agreed: gold_source existing_metadata (p. 3), gold_beyond_stimulus yes (p. 5, Test 1), gold_community_dependent no, gold_concerns_genesis no, answer_multiplicity single_answer (p. 3), plurality_treatment not_stated. cip's facets_explanation rightly notes that the 'domain experts' remark (p. 2) is generic, so existing_metadata rests on the labels being lifted from existing records. dataset_size 3445 = 1,864 + 863 + 718 (p. 3); both readers agreed.
